spring.title: Spring at Kingfisher Hollow
spring.intro: At Kingfisher Hollow, spring starts with water and light. Rain and thaw wet the low ground while sunlight still reaches the forest floor. Woodland flowers, their insect visitors, and animals moving to breed in water respond to different parts of that change.
spring.next_observation: How long does spring light reach the forest floor? Revisit the same stretch of woods as the canopy fills in and see where flowers and their visitors are still active.

passages.title: Where water gathers
passages.body: Rain and thaw collect in low places. In New York woodlands, pools that dry later in the year can give frogs and salamanders breeding water with fewer fish predators. Some of the small crustaceans in those pools lay eggs that survive the dry months and hatch when water returns.
passages.look_for: Where rainwater collects, compare shallow water with the deeper pond margin from firm ground. Look for egg masses and for movement in open water and among stems.

passages.title: A short window of woodland light
passages.body: Before trees leaf out, sunlight reaches the litter and warms the ground. Some woodland herbs grow and flower in that brief window, bringing pollen and nectar within reach of spring-active bees and flies. Other woodland plants flower later, as the first leaves begin to cast shade.
passages.look_for: Compare flowers in a sunny opening and beneath trees that have begun to leaf out. Which flowers have visitors in each setting?

passages.title: Life moves into the leaves and stems
passages.body: As the canopy fills, spring adds fresh leaves and stems. Caterpillars can feed on young foliage, while plants along water margins give aquatic insects cover and, for emerging dragonflies, a way out of the water. By late spring, the woods and pond margins are offering different kinds of food and shelter.
passages.look_for: Look for new leaves with holes, folds, or fine trails inside the leaf. At the pond, notice which insects move among stems and which fly over open water.

rows.name: Spotted Salamander
rows.interpretation: Spotted salamanders lay their eggs in jelly-covered masses in spring pools. Green algae can grow inside the masses and supply oxygen as the embryos develop.

sources.label: Experimental study of algae in spotted salamander eggs

rows.name: Clemens’ Agonopterix
rows.interpretation: Clemens’ Agonopterix survives winter as an adult and can fly again when the weather warms. Its caterpillars feed inside folded leaves of carrot-family plants.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks account of Clemens’ Agonopterix
Tompkins County study of Clemens’ Agonopterix host plants

rows.name: yellow trout lily
rows.interpretation: Yellow trout lilies use the short stretch of sunlight between snowmelt and canopy closure. After the flowers set seed, ants carry the seeds away for the rich morsel attached to each one.

sources.label: Research on the trout lily’s spring light window
Duke Gardens on trout lily and seed dispersal by ants

rows.name: northern starflower
rows.interpretation: In late spring, northern starflower lifts white blooms above a ring of leaves. The plant also spreads below ground, where tubers send up new shoots.

sources.label: Kasey Hartz Natural Area account of northern starflower

rows.name: Gray Treefrog
rows.interpretation: From late spring, male gray treefrogs trill from shrubs and branches near breeding water. Broad toe pads help them grip the stems and branches they climb.

sources.label: Maryland DNR on gray treefrog calls and habitat

rows.name: Common Baskettail
rows.interpretation: Common Baskettails patrol pond margins in late spring and early summer. A female carries a cluster of eggs at the tip of her abdomen and deposits it among floating plants or algae.

sources.label: University of Nebraska State Museum on baskettail patrols and season
Wisconsin Odonata Survey on Common Baskettail egg laying

bird_examples.name: Rusty Blackbird
bird_examples.note: This April checklist records Rusty Blackbird at Kingfisher Hollow on one visit.

summer.title: Summer at Kingfisher Hollow
summer.intro: Summer at the Hollow takes different forms in the pond, the moving creek, and the woods and sunny edges around them. Insects that hunt by day, moths that fly after dusk, and the plants their young feed on are part of the same summer community.
summer.next_observation: What changes at an edge between afternoon and dusk? Watch the same patch of pond bank and vegetation at both times, and see which animals move over the water or among the stems.

passages.title: Still water and current
passages.body: Still water and current offer different places for young animals to live. In a pond, shallow vegetation gives tadpoles and aquatic insects places to feed or hide. In a creek, stones and quieter pockets along the bank give aquatic insects places to hold on or get out of the main current.
passages.look_for: Compare quiet water among pond stems with the moving water around creek stones. From the bank, notice where surface insects gather and where small animals hold their place in the current.

passages.title: The summer moth community
passages.body: Summer moth diversity starts with what caterpillars eat. Some feed openly on foliage. Others mine between a leaf’s surfaces, feed from inside a fold, or bore into shoots. The plants in the woods and open edges help determine which caterpillars can live there. Different adults fly at different points in the season, so the mix of moths changes through summer.
passages.look_for: Look for the work of different leaf feeders in daylight. A winding trail inside a leaf, an edge rolled into a shelter, and a leaf chewed from the outside each show a different way of feeding.

passages.title: How vegetation feeds the summer community
passages.body: With the canopy in full leaf, the shaded woods and sunny edges offer different food. Flowering herbs draw insects that feed on pollen and nectar, while foliage feeds caterpillars that can in turn feed nestlings. Streamside plants provide cover at the boundary between water and land.
passages.look_for: Choose a spot where shade meets sun. Notice which insects use flowers, which stay among leaves, and where birds search the vegetation for food.

rows.name: Eastern Pondhawk
rows.interpretation: Eastern Pondhawks hunt around ponds and other slow water in summer. They launch from low perches and can catch flying insects nearly their own size.

sources.label: Wisconsin Odonata Survey on Eastern Pondhawk
North Carolina State Parks dragonfly accounts

rows.name: Pickerel Frog
rows.interpretation: Pickerel frogs favor cool, wooded streams in summer and also leave the water to feed in nearby grassy openings.

sources.label: Minnesota DNR on Pickerel Frog summer habitat

rows.name: Lettered Habrosyne Moth
rows.interpretation: Adult Lettered Habrosynes fly after dusk in summer. Their caterpillars eat blackberry leaves, so the brambles at a woodland edge can support another stage of the same moth.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks on Lettered Habrosyne host plants
Summer night encounter at Kingfisher Hollow

rows.name: arrow-leaved tearthumb
rows.interpretation: Arrow-leaved tearthumb scrambles over neighboring stems in wet places, helped by tiny backward-pointing prickles. Clusters of pale flowers open from midsummer into early autumn.

sources.label: University of Michigan on how arrow-leaved tearthumb climbs
Michigan State University on tearthumb flowering

rows.name: Calico Crayfish
rows.interpretation: Calico crayfish use underwater vegetation for cover in slow water. As water recedes, they can retreat into burrows.

sources.label: Michigan DNR field guide to crayfish

autumn.title: Autumn at Kingfisher Hollow
autumn.intro: Autumn changes what the Hollow offers to animals. Late flowers keep some insects fed, seeds and fruits carry food later into the season, and falling leaves bring fresh material to the forest floor and creek.
autumn.next_observation: Where do fallen leaves come to rest after a rain? Follow the change from dry leaf litter to wet streamside piles and see where leaves are still whole and where they are already breaking apart.

passages.title: Food changes at the edge
passages.body: Flowering along open edges can continue as trees begin to change color. Late blooms offer pollen and nectar on days when insects can still fly. As flowers go to seed and shrubs bear fruit, the edge offers different food to animals that remain or pass through.
passages.look_for: Compare open flowers with dry seed heads and fruiting shrubs. Notice whether the same patch is used by flower visitors, seed-eating birds, or both.

passages.title: Leaves and wood feed another community
passages.body: Fallen leaves join wood already breaking down in the forest. Fungi work through dead branches and logs, and some produce fruiting bodies on the surface. Leaves that reach the creek feed a different community of decomposers and aquatic insects that break the litter into smaller pieces.
passages.look_for: Compare the fungi on solid wood with those on soft, crumbling logs. Along the creek, look for whole leaves caught in quiet pockets and softer leaves breaking into pieces.

passages.title: Preparing for the cold
passages.body: Mild afternoons and evenings can still bring flying insects after many leaves are down. Other insects are already spending the season as eggs, larvae, pupae, or adults in sheltered places. The stems, leaves, and bark that supported summer activity can also provide winter cover.
passages.look_for: On a mild afternoon, watch for insects where the sun warms bare ground or a sheltered edge. In the shade, look for intact stems, loose bark, and leaf piles that will hold cover through winter.

rows.name: wrinkle-leaved goldenrod
rows.interpretation: Wrinkle-leaved goldenrod opens sprays of small yellow flowers as summer turns to autumn. Bees and other insects feed on the nectar and pollen, and birds can eat the seeds that follow.

sources.label: USDA plant guide to wrinkle-leaved goldenrod

rows.name: Pear-shaped Puffball
rows.interpretation: Pear-shaped puffballs fruit in clusters on decaying logs and stumps in autumn. A pore opens at the top as each puffball ripens, releasing a cloud of spores when raindrops strike it.

sources.label: Ohio DNR field guide to stump puffballs

rows.name: Conifer Mazegill
rows.interpretation: Conifer Mazegill breaks down dead wood, especially conifers, leaving a brown rot. Its tough shelves can persist after leaf fall, with gill-like folds beneath.

sources.label: NC State Mycological Herbarium on Conifer Mazegill
Natural Resources Canada on Conifer Mazegill and brown rot

rows.name: Autumn Meadowhawk
rows.interpretation: Autumn Meadowhawks can bask on bare ground on cool days, then dart after small flying insects. Sun-warmed perches help them stay active well into autumn.

sources.label: Illinois DNR on Autumn Meadowhawk behavior
University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee Field Station on late flight

rows.name: Bicolored Sallow
rows.interpretation: Bicolored Sallows fly well into autumn. In spring, their young caterpillars can feed on opening red maple buds.

sources.label: North Carolina State Parks account of Bicolored Sallow
Bucknell University research on goldenrod and its insects
USDA plant guide to wrinkle-leaved goldenrod

winter.title: Winter at Kingfisher Hollow
winter.intro: Leaf fall opens the view between the pond, creek, and slope woods. Snow can reveal animals still moving, while bark, litter, standing stems, and water shelter life through the cold months.
winter.next_observation: Which parts of the Hollow still offer food and cover in winter? Compare a sheltered woodland edge with a stretch of creek, looking for standing seeds, feeding birds, and tracks where the two settings meet.

passages.title: What winter leaves standing
passages.body: With the hardwood canopy bare, evergreen trees, standing stems, and fallen wood are easier to see. Conifer boughs provide cover, seed heads can still hold food, and fallen leaves shelter small animals. Along the creek and pond, snow and ice make the difference between still water and current visible.
passages.look_for: From a safe bank, notice which parts of the pond or creek carry snow on ice and where water is open. In the woods, compare the cover under evergreens with the open ground under bare trees.

passages.title: Life above and below the waterline
passages.body: Winter shelter depends on the animal and its stage of life. Some insects wait out the cold under bark or in litter as eggs, pupae, or adults. Many stream insects spend winter underwater as larvae, and in eastern streams a few kinds even emerge as adults during the cold months.
passages.look_for: Notice where bark crevices, dead stems, and accumulated leaves offer small pockets of shelter. At open water, look from the bank for insect movement without lifting bark or overturning stones.

passages.title: Following food and cover
passages.body: Some animals stay active and move among the food and shelter winter leaves available. Snow can trace mammals along banks and over fallen wood. Birds use the same landscape at a different height, feeding among seed heads, probing bark for insects, or searching branches and twigs.
passages.look_for: Look for paired or single-file prints in fresh snow, then watch where birds feed. Which activity stays close to the ground, and which follows bark, branches, or standing stems?

rows.name: Western Conifer Seed Bug
rows.interpretation: Adult Western Conifer Seed Bugs leave their feeding grounds on conifer cones in autumn and pass the winter under loose bark or in sheltered crevices, including in buildings.

sources.label: US Forest Service field guide to Western Conifer Seed Bug
Penn State Extension on Western Conifer Seed Bug life history

rows.name: American Mink
rows.interpretation: American mink hunt fish in winter and can surface through openings in stream ice. On snowy banks, their loping gait often leaves paired prints.

sources.label: New York State DEC on mink foraging and tracks

rows.name: Fisher
rows.interpretation: Fishers travel over snow in a bounding gait that often leaves prints in pairs. They mate in late winter and early spring, with young born around the same season the following year.

sources.label: New York State DEC on identifying Fisher signs

rows.name: Gray Fox
rows.interpretation: Gray foxes stay active on winter nights, hunting mice and rabbits. They can also climb trees by gripping the trunk with their front feet and pushing upward with their hind feet.

sources.label: US Forest Service on gray fox diet and winter activity
New York State DEC on gray fox climbing
